parts: Lesson 11: Play and Early Learning — Summary

Play is a creative process in which a child uses mind and body free from externally imposed goals — a freely chosen engagement with objects, peers or oneself that allows exploring, experimenting and experiencing without threat. Piaget: responses repeated purely for functional pleasure; Froebel: highly serious and of deep significance. Definitions: Ross — joyful, spontaneous, creative activity in which man finds his fullest expression; Gross — instinctive practice of activities essential later in life; Stern — a free, self-contained activity driven by intrinsic motivation; Montessori — play is the work of the child; Hurlock — any activity directed to an end other than enjoyment is not play.

Physical: exercises the body, uses surplus energy, coordinates muscles. Social: friendships, cooperation, manners, solving problems with friends. Cognitive: observing, concentrating, experimenting, problem solving, vocabulary, imagination, creativity. Moral: right and wrong, respect for elders, behaviour with peers. Therapeutic: releases pent-up emotions; shy children open up, aggressive ones learn to wait, over-competitive ones accept losses. Recreational: enjoyment, relaxation, no boredom. Educational: colours, sizes, shapes and textures through toys. Research (Sergio Pellis) shows play changes neural connections in the front of the brain.

Piaget: practice play (sensorimotor stage, 0–2: repeated body movements, mouthing objects); symbolic play (2–7: an object stands for something else, make-believe and role play); games with rules (7–11: structured, social play). Smilansky: functional play (first stage — playing with objects, physical movements); constructive play (using objects to build something); dramatic play (using imagination); games with rules (competitive games accepting rules).

Parten's six social stages: unoccupied play (0–2, not really playing); solitary play (alone, common in young toddlers); onlooker play (watches others without joining, about 2½–3½ years); parallel play (side by side with similar toys, not together, about 2½–3½); associative play (3–4 years: play together but without a common goal or rules); cooperative play (organised groups, teamwork, leaders and roles, group goals).

First two years: sensorimotor play, play with objects (from 4–5 months, once eye-hand coordination allows grasping), symbolic play after the first year (a wooden block as a telephone), social play with adults from about 1½ years. Two to five years: play becomes purposeful; groups grow; playmates chosen by age and gender; solitary and parallel play; make-believe and dramatic play (shopkeeper, family roles). Five to twelve: systematic, logical, rule-bound competitive games such as football and basketball.

Materials must be attractive and accessible; open spaces allow free movement; adults should be present; mere display on shelves frustrates children. Points to keep in mind: ease of supervision, safety, space for free movement, children's interests, needs of the group and of each child, special activities placed handy, similar activities together, furniture of suitable size and height.

Indoor areas: dolls corner/dramatic area (role play with home objects); blocks or construction area (heavy blocks on low shelves; builds imagination, creativity, social and motor skills); library, books and puzzle area (well lit, low furniture); art area (near water); also discovery, music and movement corners. Toys: for physical movement, for constructive and creative play, and for dramatic and fantasy play, graded by age (birth–2: swings, large balls, pull-along toys; 2–4: blocks, picture books, puzzles, kitchen kits, drawing; 4–6: balance beams, water play, group games, slides and merry-go-rounds). Outdoor: tricycle paths, sand pit, water play, jungle gym, slides and swings, open green space; outdoor play needs supervision. Groups: large (circle time, stories, music), medium (10–12 children), small (fewer than six, for individual attention).

Cognitive and language: sense games, concept formation (colour, shape, size, number), puzzles, story and picture completion, memory games, sequencing, arranging objects by size, matching pictures, observing nature; for language — conversation, stories, role play, puppets, listening games. Affective: dramatising stories, singing, reciting poems in rhythm, dressing dolls, group celebrations. Psychomotor: gross — pushing, pulling, throwing, catching, pedalling, jumping, swinging; fine — stringing beads, printing, tearing, cutting, collage, clay. Thematic planning: themes from the child's environment (myself, family, food, water, seasons, people who help me) for a week or two.

Observer (watches interaction and use of materials to plan better play), facilitator (arranges equipment, lets children speak and ask questions), reviewer (checks whether play met each child's needs and the curriculum goals and informs parents) and organiser (prepares a safe, happy, challenging play environment and materials).
